conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with some epigastric pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about a week ago. I had a cold—just congestion and a dry cough—and then this pressure in my upper belly began. It doesn’t move anywhere, and it’s not sharp, just a constant discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Does it get worse after eating? Or when you lie down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little worse after meals, and I’ve been burping a lot. It feels gassy. But it goes away when I sleep. I took aspirin before coming because this pain… it’s the same one I had before my heart surgery last year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Because of your history—CABG and prior heart issues—we take any recurring pain like this seriously. We’ve checked your cardiac enzymes three times, and all were negative. No sign of a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank goodness. But why would it come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG showed minor changes—some T-wave inversion and ST depression—but no active ischemia. Given that you’re not having chest pain, shortness of breath, or sweating, and the labs are clear, we think this is likely related to acid reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Heartburn? But it feels just like the pain before my heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And that’s why we admitted you. For patients with heart disease, stomach pain can be an ‘anginal equivalent’—meaning your heart issues can present as belly discomfort. But everything we’ve seen so far points away from your heart being the cause this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… so what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a heart monitor, and we’ve done a chest X-ray—no fluid in the lungs, heart size is normal. We’ll keep you overnight for observation. We’re continuing your usual meds: aspirin, metoprolol, atorvastatin, and lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been really anxious lately—worried about money. Could that make the pain worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Anxiety can amplify physical symptoms, especially stomach discomfort. We’ve noted that, and a chaplain visited you earlier. We’ll make sure you have support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve been asymptomatic since admission, and your repeat labs are stable. Troponins stayed negative, kidney function is good. We’re confident this wasn’t a cardiac event.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s really just indigestion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely, yes. Given your frequent burping and the timing with meals, we believe it’s gastroesophageal reflux. We gave you ranitidine in the hospital and recommend you start over-the-counter Prilosec when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. Are any of my other medicines changing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching your metoprolol to the extended-release version for smoother coverage, and we’re cutting your atorvastatin dose to 40 mg daily since your LDL came back at 41—excellent control. Everything else stays the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds manageable. And if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, or the pain radiates, go to the ER immediately. But if it’s just belly discomfort with burping, try the Prilosec and see if it settles. Follow up with your primary doctor in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go home. Your condition is stable, and all signs point to resolved, non-cardiac epigastric pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better knowing my heart’s okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep taking your medications as prescribed, use the Prilosec for heartburn, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
